_source: Built from the table of contents, abstract and text of the thesis PDF (main.pdf, 350 pages). Replace this file to swap in a different mind map; keep the same shape: { root: { label, note?, children: [{ label, note?, ref?, post?, open?, children? }] } }. 'post' is a blog slug; it only renders as a link if that post is published.

root.label: ENSO, climate variability and peatland fire hotspots

children.label: Why Bengkalis
children.note: 11 sub-districts, about 511 thousand ha of mapped peat; 4,981 of Riau's 30,988 MODIS detections in 2015–2024

children.label: Problem
children.note: No sub-district-scale, statistically defensible estimate of ENSO and drought effects, their spatial variation, the predictive value of climate, or early-warning skill

children.label: RQ1 Patterns
children.note: Spatial and temporal hotspot patterns, and distribution across peat depth classes

children.label: RQ2 Climate drivers
children.note: ONI, DMI, SPI-3, SPEI-3: is the ENSO effect mediated by local water deficit?

children.label: RQ3 Heterogeneity
children.note: Does the ENSO response differ between sub-districts?

children.label: RQ4 Prediction
children.note: Contribution of climatic, seasonal, biophysical and anthropogenic factors; generalisation to unseen sub-districts and years

children.label: RQ5 Early warning
children.note: Does an ENSO-and-drought rule beat a seasonal-calendar alarm, and what follows for disaster risk management?

children.label: Scope
children.note: January 2015 to December 2024; unit of analysis is the sub-district-month; 2025 held out for an out-of-time check

children.label: Satellite hotspots as a fire proxy
Disaster-management framework
children.note: BPBD, alert and emergency statuses, national fire-danger and hotspot services

children.label: ML rarely validated against climatology across unseen years
Warning rules rarely verified against a seasonal calendar
Eight-stage workflow
children.note: Acquisition, ENSO and drought indices, filtering, panel, statistics, non-climatic factors, machine learning, early-warning skill and validation

children.label: Data
children.note: NASA FIRMS MODIS, CHIRPS v2.0, ERA5-Land, ONI and DMI, peat map, land-use layers, burned-area products

children.label: ENSO classification
children.note: NOAA five-month rule: 44 El Niño, 30 La Niña, 46 Neutral months

children.label: Drought indices
children.note: SPI-3 and SPEI-3 fitted per calendar month on a 1991–2024 baseline

children.label: Hotspot filtering
children.note: Confidence-anchored DBSCAN: anchors at 70% or more, rescue 50–69% within 1.5 km

children.label: Panel construction
children.note: 11 sub-districts × 120 months = 1,320 rows

children.label: Statistical analysis
children.note: Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn, effective-N correlation, Poisson count models, heterogeneity, trend, depth preference

children.label: Spatial and spatiotemporal analysis
children.note: Moran's I, LISA, ST-DBSCAN

children.label: Machine learning
children.note: Random Forest and XGBoost; leave-one-sub-district-out and leave-one-year-out; ablation; SHAP

children.label: Early-warning skill assessment
children.note: Nested leave-one-year-out; POD, FAR, PSS

children.label: Hotspot proxy validation
children.note: Tier 1 MODIS MCD64A1; Tier 2 Landsat dNBR and dATBI

children.label: Hotspot filtering and data overview
children.note: 5,386 points inside the regency, 3,402 retained; 91.1% on peat

children.label: Temporal patterns
children.note: Peaks in 2015 and 2019; February–March 43.4% and June–September 38.4% of hotspots; no significant annual trend (Mann–Kendall τ = −0.47, p = 0.074)

children.label: Hotspots and peat depth
children.note: Over-represented on 100–200 cm and 500–700 cm peat (Cramér's V = 0.22)

children.label: Spatial distribution
children.note: Concentrated in Rupat and Bandar Laksamana

children.label: Count models and mediation by drought
children.note: ONI IRR 1.95 per +1 °C; 1.29 after adding SPEI-3 (IRR 0.35)

children.label: Heterogeneity between sub-districts
children.note: Wald χ² = 23.2 on 10 d.f., p = 0.010

children.label: Non-climatic factors
children.note: Oil palm and forest loss correlate negatively with hotspots; not significant at sub-district level after correction

children.label: Spatial generalisation (LOKO-CV)
children.note: Pooled AUC 0.79

children.label: Temporal generalisation (LOYO-CV)
children.note: AUC 0.81; Brier skill score 0.21 against climatology

children.label: Feature contributions
children.note: Climate removed: pooled AUC 0.795 falls to 0.703; climate holds 59.1% of mean |SHAP|

children.label: Weak climate link: Pinggir and Bathin Solapan
Early-warning skill
children.note: PSS 0.21 for the ONI-plus-drought rule against 0.16 for an alarm in every fire month; ΔPSS +0.034, 95% CI −0.039 to +0.102

children.label: Drainage canals and fire location
children.note: 95.9% of hotspots within 1 km of a canal against 79.4% of peat area; odds ratio 0.74 per ten-fold distance

children.label: Validity of hotspots as a fire proxy
Tier 1: agreement with MODIS burned area
Tier 2: a Landsat burn index without fire detections
How much burned area do hotspots account for?
ENSO as an indirect, drought-mediated driver
A bimodal fire regime
children.note: Two activation windows, not one dry season

children.label: Spatial heterogeneity and land management
children.note: Mandau's weak ONI link reflects low power (22 hotspots), not climate independence

children.label: Value and limits of machine learning
children.note: Logistic regression is equivalent to Random Forest (AUC 0.806 versus 0.795)

children.label: Limitations
children.note: Eleven listed, including a short record, pseudo-replication and hotspots as a proxy

children.label: Conclusions
children.note: One answer for each of RQ1 to RQ5

children.label: Two-window preparedness calendar
children.note: February–April and July–August

children.label: Use ONI to escalate; SPEI-3 as near-term trigger
Prioritise canal blocking, rewetting and patrols
children.note: Rupat, Bandar Laksamana, Bengkalis, Pinggir; non-forest peat near canals

children.label: Daily FIRMS monitoring with the DBSCAN filter
children.note: Reduces false alarms from industrial sources around Duri

children.label: Time-varying land use and groundwater data
Geographically weighted or hierarchical Bayesian models
A. Data processing details
children.note: Methodological corrections, software, data and code availability

children.label: B. Supplementary results
children.note: Optimal ONI lag and warning windows; covariates per sub-district; largest space-time fire events

children.note: Steps 01 to 21, from setup and configuration to holdout SHAP scans
